subject: Pulkkinen et al. (1998)
object: In 3 patients with the lethal form of epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia (EB-PA), Pulkkinen et al. (1998) identified novel ITGB4 mutations on 5 alleles. They screened each ITGB4 exon by PCR, heteroduplex analysis and direct sequencing. One patient was homozygous for a 2-bp deletion in exon 34 (4501delTC).

subject: Pulkkinen et al. (1998)
object: Pulkkinen et al. (1998) found that a patient with lethal EB-PA was compound heterozygous for two ITGB4 mutations. The paternal allele carried a 2-bp deletion in exon 3 (120delTG). The maternal allele carried a cysteine substitution in exon 7 (C245G) in the extracellular domain, which the authors suggested may affect ligand binding or alpha6-beta4 dimerization.

subject: Pulkkinen et al. (1998)
object: In a third patient with lethal EB-PA, Pulkkinen et al. (1998) identified a paternal nonsense mutation in exon 4 of ITGB4 (Q73X). Three of the four distinct mutations were predicted to produce truncated polypeptides.

subject: Pulkkinen et al. (1998)
object: Pulkkinen et al. (1998) noted that EB-PA is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous autosomal recessive blistering disorder that includes lethal and nonlethal variants.

subject: Mellerio et al. (1998)
object: Mellerio et al. (1998) reported 2 unrelated patients with junctional epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia who survived into early childhood and had mild skin involvement. This differed from the usual course of the disorder, which is often fatal within the first weeks or months of life even after surgical correction.

subject: Mellerio et al. (1998)
object: In a patient with mild pyloric atresia-junctional epidermolysis bullosa, Mellerio et al. (1998) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the ITGB4 gene: a splice site mutation in exon 30 (3793+1G-A) and a nonsense mutation in exon 36 (W1478X). The authors suggested that the nonsense mutation would markedly reduce beta-4 integrin mRNA, but that the splice site allele might still allow some functional, though altered, beta-4 polypeptide to be made.

subject: Mellerio et al. (1998)
object: In a second, unrelated patient with mild pyloric atresia-junctional epidermolysis bullosa, Mellerio et al. (1998) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the ITGB4 gene: a missense mutation in exon 3 (C38R) and a 1-bp deletion in exon 36 (4776delG). The authors suggested that the missense allele might allow some functional beta-4 integrin to be synthesized, which could explain the mild phenotype.

subject: Inoue et al. (2000)
object: Inoue et al. (2000) identified a homozygous missense mutation, G931D, in the cytoplasmic tail of beta-4 integrin in non-Herlitz junctional epidermolysis bullosa without pyloric atresia. They reported that the mutation disrupted hemidesmosome assembly.

subject: Jonkman et al. (2002)
object: Jonkman et al. (2002) reported a 49-year-old woman who had mild blistering of the hands and feet from birth, nail dystrophy with onychogryposis, and enamel hypoplasia. She had no alopecia and no history of pyloric atresia. Electron microscopy and antigen mapping of a skin blister showed that the split was intraepidermal, low in the basal keratinocytes through the attachment plaque of the hemidesmosome. The authors described the phenotype as having predominant features of epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

subject: Jonkman et al. (2002)
object: In the patient, Jonkman et al. (2002) found a novel heterozygous 2-bp deletion (4733delCT) in the ITGB4 gene. The deletion caused in-frame skipping of exon 36, which was predicted to remove 50 amino acids (residues 1450-1499) within the third fibronectin type III repeat of the beta-4 cytoplasmic domain. Immunoblot analysis showed a beta-4 polypeptide 5 kDa shorter than normal. Because no full-size protein was detected in vitro and the 450-11A epitope was absent in vivo, the authors expected the patient to also be heterozygous for a null allele.

subject: Jonkman et al. (2002)
object: Jonkman et al. (2002) used immunofluorescence microscopy of the patient's skin. Monoclonal antibody 450-11A, which recognizes the third fibronectin III repeat in the intracellular domain of integrin beta-4, did not bind at all. Binding of monoclonal antibodies against epitopes at the amino- and carboxy-terminal ends of the protein was reduced.

subject: Jonkman et al. (2002)
object: Jonkman et al. (2002) concluded that deleting the third fibronectin type III repeat in the integrin beta-4 cytoplasmic domain is clinically pathogenic. This repeat is thought to interact with BP180/type XVII collagen. They concluded that its loss results in a mild phenotype with predominant features of epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

subject: Has et al. (2020)
object: Has et al. (2020) reported an international expert consensus reclassification of inherited epidermolysis bullosa (EB), which updated the 2014 classification using new clinical and molecular data. The authors introduced the concept of genetic disorders with skin fragility, with classical EB as the prototype. They classified other skin fragility disorders, such as peeling skin, erosive, hyperkeratotic and connective tissue disorders, as separate 'EB-related' categories.
